[PATCH v2] mm: free the swap slot of a dirty swapin folio

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch addresses an issue where dirty swapin folios are not properly cleaned up, leading to increased exit times and performance degradation in certain workloads. The problem arises when a folio is dirtied but its swap cache slot remains reserved until the folio is reclaimed or its owner exits. To fix this, the patch modifies the do_swap_page function to free the swap cache of dirty folios as well, which reduces the number of folios left in the swap cache and improves performance. The change has been tested on a production workload and a microbenchmark, showing significant improvements in exit times and throughput.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] KVM: arm64: Reduce the stage-2 page cache on 64 KiB hosts

version_history.subject: [PATCH] KVM: arm64: Reduce the stage-2 page cache on 64 KiB hosts

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch reduces the size of the stage-2 page cache in KVM for arm64 hosts with 64 KiB pages, from 40 to 8 entries. This change is motivated by the observation that most of the cached pages are never used and the actual memory requirements are much lower than previously assumed. The new value still covers the minimum required for a stage-2 fault and leaves room for additional table allocations. The patch affects only arm64 hosts with 64 KiB pages, leaving other configurations unchanged.

On Tue, Nov 24, 2026 at 07:28:42AM -0800, Usama Arif wrote:
> When a stage-2 fault may need new page tables, KVM first tops up the
> vCPU's page cache: if it holds fewer pages than the fault might need, it
> is refilled to KVM_ARCH_NR_OBJS_PER_MEMORY_CACHE, which arm64 sets to
> 40. Unused pages stay in the cache until the vCPU is destroyed.
> 
> With 64 KiB pages, that is 2.5 MiB per vCPU, and most of it is never
> used. Stage-2 has at most three levels and the root is preallocated, so
> a fault needs at most two new table pages (kvm_mmu_cache_min_pages()).
> As every last-level table covers 512 MiB, an 8 GiB guest needs just 17
> table pages to map all of its memory, while its four vCPU caches get
> filled with 160.
> 
> On a production host with 64 KiB pages running 101 VMs with four vCPUs
> each, the caches were still 86% full. The memory used:
> 
>                         before      after
>   per-vCPU capacity     2.5 MB     512 KB
>   all 404 vCPUs         869 MB     <= 202 MB
> 
> Let's lower the capacity to 8 with 64 KiB pages, In the production
> usecase above, it frees at least 667 MB. That still covers the two-page
> minimum and leaves room for several table allocations per refill. 4 KB
> and 16 KB pages keep 40.
> 
> The temporary cache in kvm_phys_addr_ioremap() uses the same capacity,
> but it is topped up before every page it maps, so 8 is sufficient there
> as well. The pKVM hypervisor memcache and the eager split cache don't
> use this capacity.
> 
> Signed-off-by: Usama Arif <usama.arif@linux.dev>
> ---
>  arch/arm64/include/asm/kvm_types.h | 5 +++++
>  1 file changed, 5 insertions(+)
>

> index 9a126b9e2d7c99..28568da9ea4a7b 100644

> @@ -2,7 +2,12 @@
>  #ifndef _ASM_ARM64_KVM_TYPES_H
>  #define _ASM_ARM64_KVM_TYPES_H
>  
> +/* Must cover kvm_mmu_cache_min_pages(), at most 2 with 64 KiB pages. */
> +#ifdef CONFIG_ARM64_64K_PAGES
> +#define KVM_ARCH_NR_OBJS_PER_MEMORY_CACHE 8
> +#else
>  #define KVM_ARCH_NR_OBJS_PER_MEMORY_CACHE 40
> +#endif
>  
>  #endif /* _ASM_ARM64_KVM_TYPES_H */
>  
> -- 
> 2.53.1-Meta
> 

Hi Usama,

Have you tried to reproduce this issue in v7.4-rc1 or newer?

IIUC Lorenzo Stoakes introduced a change that would cause the memcache to 
skip topup if the cache contains a minimum of ~4 pages, so it can possibly 
improve that issue.

Although I can see that when it's below that minimum it fills the whole 
capacity (40) of the cache.

In any case, Lorenzo, could you advise?

CC:Lorenzo Stoakes (ARM) (ljs@kernel.org) 

Thanks,
Leo

Right,

I took a look in the cache workings, and it does not seem to receive freed 
pages back in. It gets filled by topup and used by map, so IIUC it is used 
only to avoid failing an allocation during the mapping walk.

Maybe it could be the case to simplify this cache to have the capacity 
about the same as the minimum (since it always topup before mapping) and 
avoid the waste altogether.

Maymbe having something like this should be enough?
 
#define KVM_ARCH_NR_OBJS_PER_MEMORY_CACHE (KVM_PGTABLE_LAST_LEVEL - KVM_PGTABLE_FIRST_LEVEL)

Thanks!
Leo

IIUC, every time we topup, we call a mmu_memory_cache_alloc_obj() for every 
one of the objects in the array. So as it is today it runs it 40 times, and 
waits until it runs down to allocate up to 40 again.

With the change, it will run 4, then up to 4 how many times are needed.

So having a smaller cache can potentially save both cputime and memory if 
the cache is not that oftenly used. That being said, allocating 40 in 
sequence would be faster than 4 * 10 because the instruction / data cache 
is hot.

I think the only way to evaluate the performance impact is by running some 
benchmarks.

memory.

From: Usama Arif <usama.arif@linux.dev>
Date: Wed, 25 Nov 2026 12:55:15 -0800
Subject: [PATCH] KVM: arm64: Shrink the stage-2 memcache to the page-table
 depth

When a stage-2 fault may need new page tables, KVM first tops up the
vCPU's memcache: if it holds fewer pages than the fault might need, it
is refilled to KVM_ARCH_NR_OBJS_PER_MEMORY_CACHE, which arm64 sets to
40. Pages never return to the cache, and unused ones stay there until
the vCPU is destroyed.

The cache only has to cover a single map: every fault that can allocate
tables tops it up first, and a map allocates at most one table per
level below the preallocated root (kvm_mmu_cache_min_pages()). That is
at most three pages with 4 KiB and 16 KiB pages, and two with 64 KiB
pages.

With 64 KiB pages, the 40-page cache is 2.5 MiB per vCPU. As every
last-level table covers 512 MiB, an 8 GiB guest needs just 17 table
pages to map all of its memory, while its four vCPU caches get filled
with 160. On a production host with 64 KiB pages running 101 VMs with
four vCPUs each, the caches were still 86% full. The memory used:

                        before      after
  per-vCPU capacity     2.5 MiB     256 KiB
  all 404 vCPUs         869 MiB     <= 101 MiB

Let's size the cache to KVM_PGTABLE_LAST_LEVEL - KVM_PGTABLE_FIRST_LEVEL,
which is 4 pages and covers the deepest walk with one page to spare. On
the host above, it frees at least 768 MiB. Refills get more frequent,
but no more than four pages per vCPU ever sit unused. With 4 KiB pages,
the cache shrinks from 160 KiB to 16 KiB per vCPU.

Move the two level definitions to asm/kvm_types.h, so that the generic
top-up code in kvm_main.c can see them. kvm_pgtable.h still gets them
through linux/kvm_types.h.

The temporary cache in kvm_phys_addr_ioremap() uses the same capacity,
but it is topped up before every page it maps. The pKVM hypervisor
memcache and the eager split cache don't use this capacity.

The cost also scales with vCPUs, not with guest memory: up to 2.5 MB

every translation fault tops the cache up to kvm_mmu_cache_min_pages()
before taking mmu_lock, and a single map never needs more than that.

capacity at its first refill, but nothing requires that to be a
compile-time constant. Does something like the patch below work for
you? Each VM records twice the largest kvm_mmu_cache_min_pages() of its
stage-2s as they are initialised, and every top-up passes that to

>From dad1d43f1c2dcb8ffbc8084ec19467731e8548f4 Mon Sep 17 00:00:00 2001
From: Usama Arif <usama.arif@linux.dev>
Date: Fri, 27 Nov 2026 06:07:35 -0800
Subject: [PATCH] KVM: arm64: Size the stage-2 memcache from
 kvm_mmu_cache_min_pages()

When fewer than kvm_mmu_cache_min_pages() pages are left, a stage-2
fault that may need new tables refills the vCPU's memcache to
KVM_ARCH_NR_OBJS_PER_MEMORY_CACHE, 40 on arm64. A map allocates at most
one table per level below the preallocated root, which is
kvm_mmu_cache_min_pages() and at most 3 pages. Only vCPU destruction
frees the memcache, so whatever a refill leaves unused stays allocated:
up to 2.5 MiB per vCPU with 64 KiB pages. On a 64 KiB host running 101
VMs with 4 vCPUs and 1 GiB each, the memcaches held 986 MiB, against
25 MiB of stage-2 tables in use.

Size the memcache at twice the largest kvm_mmu_cache_min_pages() of the
VM's stage-2s instead, so that each refill covers at least two
worst-case maps. With NV, the vCPU's memcache also feeds the shadow
stage-2s, and a memcache's capacity can't change once used, so record
the largest value as each stage-2 is initialised. The VM's stage-2 is
set up at VM creation and the first shadow stage-2s by the first
KVM_ARM_VCPU_INIT, before any vCPU can fault, and later shadow stage-2s
have the same size. kvm_phys_addr_ioremap()'s temporary memcache uses
the same capacity, so arm64 no longer uses the value of
KVM_ARCH_NR_OBJS_PER_MEMORY_CACHE.

With a 48-bit IPA, the capacity is 4 pages with 16 KiB and 64 KiB pages
and 6 with 4 KiB pages; with the default 40-bit IPA, 2 and 4. On the
host above and on a production host also running 101 VMs with 4 vCPUs
each, both with 64 KiB pages and 48-bit IPA VMs:

                     memcaches                saved
                     before      after
  host above         986 MiB     81 MiB       905 MiB
  production host    869 MiB     <= 101 MiB   >= 768 MiB

A memcache now refills at most once every two tables, as a capacity of
4 does with 4 KiB pages and a 48-bit IPA. Measured that way, per fault
for the median vCPU, one VM at a time:

                                        40           4
  2M blocks split under dirty logging   4.9-5.1 us   4.9-5.0 us
  1G block split, then refaulted        2.7-2.8 us   2.8 us
  every fault allocating a table        4.0-4.1 us   3.7-4.1 us

Suggested-by: Marc Zyngier <maz@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Usama Arif <usama.arif@linux.dev>
---
 arch/arm64/include/asm/kvm_host.h  |  2 ++
 arch/arm64/include/asm/kvm_types.h |  1 +
 arch/arm64/kvm/mmu.c               | 19 +++++++++++++++----
 3 files changed, 18 insertions(+), 4 deletions(-)

diff --git a/arch/arm64/include/asm/kvm_host.h b/arch/arm64/include/asm/kvm_host.h
index 97332ffcb1300e..515869c190c66a 100644
--- a/arch/arm64/include/asm/kvm_host.h
+++ b/arch/arm64/include/asm/kvm_host.h
@@ -413,6 +413,8 @@ enum kvm_arm_vm_flavor {
 
 struct kvm_arch {
 	struct kvm_s2_mmu mmu;
+	/* Capacity of the vCPU stage-2 memcaches, see kvm_init_stage2_mmu() */
+	int mmu_page_cache_capacity;
 	const struct kvm_vm_s2_ops *vm_s2_ops;
 
 	enum kvm_arm_vm_flavor vm_flavor;
diff --git a/arch/arm64/include/asm/kvm_types.h b/arch/arm64/include/asm/kvm_types.h
index 9a126b9e2d7c99..68472a593578f3 100644
--- a/arch/arm64/include/asm/kvm_types.h
+++ b/arch/arm64/include/asm/kvm_types.h
@@ -2,6 +2,7 @@
 #ifndef _ASM_ARM64_KVM_TYPES_H
 #define _ASM_ARM64_KVM_TYPES_H
 
+/* Enables the generic MMU memory caches; arm64 passes its own capacity. */
 #define KVM_ARCH_NR_OBJS_PER_MEMORY_CACHE 40
 
 #endif /* _ASM_ARM64_KVM_TYPES_H */
diff --git a/arch/arm64/kvm/mmu.c b/arch/arm64/kvm/mmu.c
index 042dc53267cb36..cd0605cce45d2a 100644
--- a/arch/arm64/kvm/mmu.c
+++ b/arch/arm64/kvm/mmu.c
@@ -1045,7 +1045,7 @@ static void kvm_stage2_destroy(struct kvm_pgtable *pgt)
  */
 int kvm_init_stage2_mmu(struct kvm *kvm, struct kvm_s2_mmu *mmu, unsigned long type)
 {
-	int cpu, err;
+	int cpu, err, capacity;
 	struct kvm_pgtable *pgt;
 
 	/* Initialize the VM ops for the VM instance for the first time */
@@ -1086,6 +1086,15 @@ int kvm_init_stage2_mmu(struct kvm *kvm, struct kvm_s2_mmu *mmu, unsigned long t
 		goto out_free_pgtable;
 
 	mmu->pgt = pgt;
+
+	/*
+	 * The vCPU memcaches serve all of the VM's stage-2s and can't be
+	 * resized once used, so make them cover two maps on the deepest one.
+	 */
+	capacity = 2 * kvm_mmu_cache_min_pages(mmu);
+	if (capacity > kvm->arch.mmu_page_cache_capacity)
+		kvm->arch.mmu_page_cache_capacity = capacity;
+
 	if (is_protected_kvm_enabled())
 		return 0;
 
@@ -1317,8 +1326,9 @@ int kvm_phys_addr_ioremap(struct kvm *kvm, phys_addr_t guest_ipa,
 	guest_ipa &= PAGE_MASK;
 
 	for (addr = guest_ipa; addr < guest_ipa + size; addr += PAGE_SIZE) {
-		ret = kvm_mmu_topup_memory_cache(&cache,
-						 kvm_mmu_cache_min_pages(mmu));
+		ret = __kvm_mmu_topup_memory_cache(&cache,
+						   kvm->arch.mmu_page_cache_capacity,
+						   kvm_mmu_cache_min_pages(mmu));
 		if (ret)
 			break;
 
@@ -1669,10 +1679,11 @@ static void *get_mmu_memcache(struct kvm_vcpu *vcpu)
 
 static int topup_mmu_memcache(struct kvm_s2_mmu *mmu, void *memcache)
 {
+	int capacity = kvm_s2_mmu_to_kvm(mmu)->arch.mmu_page_cache_capacity;
 	int min_pages = kvm_mmu_cache_min_pages(mmu);
 
 	if (!is_protected_kvm_enabled())
-		return kvm_mmu_topup_memory_cache(memcache, min_pages);
+		return __kvm_mmu_topup_memory_cache(memcache, capacity, min_pages);
 
 	return topup_hyp_memcache(memcache, min_pages);
 }

On Tue, 24 Nov 2026 15:28:42 +0000,

> When a stage-2 fault may need new page tables, KVM first tops up the

>

> usecase above, it frees at least 667 MB. That still covers the two-page
> minimum and leaves room for several table allocations per refill. 4 KB
> and 16 KB pages keep 40.

I'll glance over the use of 64kB pages, because that's definitely a
niche configuration that hardly anyone uses. But the scale of the
numbers strike me a bit: 808GB worth of guest memory, and you're
complaining about 869MB? That's roughly 0.1% of the total, and the
savings you're gaining are even less... I know memory is expensive,
but you'd save a lot more than that by using a realistic page size.
Just saying...

I also question the assumption you are making that the guest is
strictly using IPA contiguous memory, and that therefore a very small
set of pages are all you need to map a guest. Guests with multiple,
disjoint memslots are (sadly) extremely common, specially in these
days of tiered memory and other random horrors.

>

> but it is topped up before every page it maps, so 8 is sufficient there

account. And then you adjust it by whatever fudge factor seems

pre-allocation than anything it seems. As per the comment above struct
kvm_mmu_memory_cache in include/linux/kvm_types.h:

 * Memory caches are used to preallocate memory ahead of various MMU flows,
 * e.g. page fault handlers.  Gracefully handling allocation failures deep in
 * MMU flows is problematic, as is triggering reclaim, I/O, etc... while
 * holding MMU locks.  Note, these caches act more like prefetch buffers than
 * classical caches, i.e. objects are not returned to the cache on being freed.

The question is would going from 40 to 3 slow things down?

At 40 you do 40 __get_free_page() calls on topup for the _first_ fault that hits
it, which adds latency to a random s2 fault (not great).

(If the fault doesn't in fact use a page table, this is only done once until a
page table is next needed).

And then as 37 page tables are mapped, those ones don't get allocations at 38
you go again...

With 3 in the cache you allocate up to 3 for each fault.

So in both cases you allocate the same amount of pages but in the 40 case it's
all bunched up on one s2 fault with a jump in latency, in the 3 case it's spread
out.

I'd say 3 is therefore the better choice.

Also, as mentioned elsewhere, you end up leaking pages once the S2 page tables
are setup until the vCPU is destroyed, as nothing clears down the cache
AFAICT. With 40 that's way more than with 3.

review_comments.raw_body:
On Thu, Nov 26, 2026 at 04:30:24PM +0000, Lorenzo Stoakes (ARM) wrote:
> I also think actually there's an existing problem with the top-up right now in
> user_mem_abort() that needs addressing too, actually, that this change exposes
> and will cause bugs if done as above.
>
> So right now top-up is conditional there:
>
> 	if (!perm_fault || memslot_is_logging(s2fd->memslot) ||
> 	    is_protected_kvm_enabled()) {
> 		ret = topup_mmu_memcache(s2fd->mmu, memcache);
> 		if (ret)
> 			return ret;
> 	}
>
> Inverted is 'permission fault && !dirty-logging && !pKVM'. So the question is
> whether a permission fault not needing a new page table is correct.
>
> So working through, the actual decision about a page table allocation is done
> in:
>
> user_mem_abort()
>   -> kvm_s2_fault_map()
>     -> kvm_pgtable_stage2_map()
>       -> ... -> stage2_map_walk_leaf()
>         -> stage2_map_walker_try_leaf()
> 	  -> stage2_leaf_mapping_allowed()
> 	    -> kvm_block_mapping_supported() [ if false, allocate a page table ]
>
> static bool kvm_block_mapping_supported(const struct kvm_pgtable_visit_ctx *ctx, u64 phys)
> {
> 	u64 granule = kvm_granule_size(ctx->level);
>
> 	...
>
> 	if (granule > (ctx->end - ctx->addr))
> 		return false;
>
> 	...
> }
>
> But page table size can vary in NV between host and guest (guest must be >=
> host) and it gets clamped to the smaller of the two in kvm_s2_resolve_vma_size():
>
> static short kvm_s2_resolve_vma_size(const struct kvm_s2_fault_desc *s2fd,
> 				     struct kvm_s2_fault_vma_info *s2vi,
> 				     struct vm_area_struct *vma)
> {
> 	...
> 	if (s2fd->nested) {
> 		...
> 		/*
> 		 * If we're about to create a shadow stage 2 entry, then we
> 		 * can only create a block mapping if the guest stage 2 page
> 		 * table uses at least as big a mapping.
> 		 */
> 		max_map_size = min(kvm_s2_trans_size(s2fd->nested), max_map_size);
> 		...
> 	}
> }
>
> This sets s2vi->vma_pagesize based on this value:
>
> static int kvm_s2_fault_get_vma_info(const struct kvm_s2_fault_desc *s2fd,
> 				     struct kvm_s2_fault_vma_info *s2vi)
> {
> 	...
> 	s2vi->vma_pagesize = BIT(kvm_s2_resolve_vma_size(s2fd, s2vi, vma));
> 	...
> }
>
> And the fault map uses this in the mapping size, which defines ctx->addr, end
> above in kvm_block_mapping_supported():
>
> static int kvm_s2_fault_map(const struct kvm_s2_fault_desc *s2fd,
> 			    const struct kvm_s2_fault_vma_info *s2vi,
> 			    enum kvm_pgtable_prot prot,
> 			    void *memcache,
> 			    struct kvm_s2_fault_result *result)
> {
> 	...
> 	mapping_size = s2vi->vma_pagesize;
> 	...
> 			ret = KVM_PGT_FN(kvm_pgtable_stage2_map)(pgt, gfn_to_gpa(gfn), mapping_size,
> 							 __pfn_to_phys(pfn), prot,
> 							 memcache, flags);
> 	...
> }
>
> So basically, if the host has smaller page table size than the guest, you need
> an extra page table level.
>
> So simple solution is to add nested to the check:
>
>         if (!perm_fault || memslot_is_logging(s2fd->memslot) ||
>             is_protected_kvm_enabled() || s2fd->nested) {
>                 ret = topup_mmu_memcache(s2fd->mmu, memcache);
>                 if (ret)
>                         return ret;
>         }
>
> But honestly I wonder at this point if it's truly worth doing all these checks?
> Maybe safer to just topup unconditionally.
>
> It'll only top up once before the cache is full anyway, so it's low cost. And
> would make more consistent with other fault paths too.

Given this is pre-existing, let me send a patch to fix this separately.

--
Cheers, Lorenzo

> When I mention cache locality above, I mean the cpu cache. Running the same
> routine 40 times in a row can be faster since all instructions are already

lost in the noise vs. zeroing each page anyway, and additionally you can argue

patches_submitted.patch_summary: The patch fixes a bug in the IBS (Intel Branch Stack) perf event on x86, where PERF_SAMPLE_WEIGHT_STRUCT samples would leak kernel stack contents to user space due to an uninitialized variable. The fix involves writing a default value for this variable.

review_comments.raw_body:
> For a load that missed the data cache, perf_ibs_parse_ld_st_data()
> reports the miss latency as the sample weight and marks
> PERF_SAMPLE_WEIGHT_TYPE as done, so perf_prepare_sample() leaves the
> field alone. With PERF_SAMPLE_WEIGHT_STRUCT it writes only var1_dw and
> var2_w, but perf_output_sample() copies all 8 bytes of the union into
> the ring buffer. var3_w therefore carries whatever was left in the
> on-stack struct perf_sample_data in perf_ibs_handle_irq().
> 
> CONFIG_INIT_STACK_ALL_ZERO hides this by clearing the struct on entry.
> Without it, every such sample hands 2 bytes of kernel stack to user
> space. "perf mem record" asks for PERF_SAMPLE_WEIGHT_STRUCT on x86, and
> since v6.14 swfilt lets an unprivileged user sample their own tasks with
> IBS.
> 
> Write var3_w as well.
>

patches_reviewed.patch_summary: This patch modifies the KVM (Kernel-based Virtual Machine) for arm64 to top up the mmu memcache on user faults, specifically when a permission fault occurs in a non-volatile memory (NV) region. The current implementation does not handle this scenario correctly, leading to potential issues with memory allocation. To address this, the patch adds a condition to top up the mmu memcache for every user fault, which covers the narrow case of a permission fault on a THP block. This change is necessary because the existing logic has limitations and conflicts with older kernel versions.
